name: Akkadian Empire (Naram-Sin)

areaKm2.note: Seshat codes Polity Territory 450,000-1,000,000 km2 for 2270-2083 BCE (mid = midpoint). Taagepera 1978 gives 0.8 million km2 at 2250 BCE (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_largest_empires). Border = union of the historical-basemaps world_bc3000 polygons 'Ur' (southern and central Mesopotamia incl. Susa, 341,000 km2) and 'city-states' (Upper Mesopotamia and north Syria incl. Mari, Nagar, Ebla, 228,000 km2), computed from the GeoJSON at ~569,000 km2; bc3000 is the nearest file at or before 2250 BCE and has no Akkad polygon.

population.note: OWID historical population (https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/population.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true, McEvedy-Jones/HYDE series): Iraq 0.5 M in 3000 BCE and 0.875 M in 2000 BCE, linear to 2250 BCE = 0.78 M; plus roughly half of Syria's 0.69 M (2000 BCE) for the Upper Mesopotamian and north Syrian provinces (Mari, Nagar, Ebla) and Susiana. Seshat codes the Akkadian population as undecided (https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/476). Wide range.

urbanization.note: Educated guess. Southern Mesopotamia was the most urban region of its time (Uruk, Ur, Lagash, Kish); the northern and Zagros provinces much less. Seshat codes the largest settlement at 20,000-40,000.

activePersonnel.note: Field force of Naram-Sin c. 2250: no modern total exists. Anchors: a Sargon inscription says 5,400 men ate daily before him, read as a standing royal army (Westenholz 1999 pp. 65-68, cited in the fetched page); Naram-Sin's inscription names the 'Nine Regiments of Akkad' as the core. Rimush claims 16,212 enemy slain in one battle (royal inscription, quoted in Hamblin 2006, not used as a size). Low = the 5,400 standing troops plus support; mid adds governors' garrisons in the subject cities and city levies for a campaign; high = a full imperial muster.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess. City levies callable within a month along the river network.

supportPersonnel.note: Educated guess. Boat crews, onager-wagon drivers, scribes and quartermasters.

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess. Agrarian temple-and-palace state with corvee obligations; Sumerian city levies were large relative to population.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Field force of Naram-Sin c. 2250: no modern total exists. Anchors: a Sargon inscription says 5,400 men ate daily before him, read as a standing royal army (Westenholz 1999 pp. 65-68, cited in the fetched page); Naram-Sin's inscription names the 'Nine Regiments of Akkad' as the core. Rimush claims 16,212 enemy slain in one battle (royal inscription, quoted in Hamblin 2006, not used as a size). Split: close-order spear, axe and mace infantry ~57%.

quality.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: copper/bronze axes, spears and maces; lighter kit than the Early Dynastic phalanx but well equipped for the era.

training.note: Core of 5,400 professionals (0.75) diluted by city levies (0.25-0.5).

count.note: Field force of Naram-Sin c. 2250: no modern total exists. Anchors: a Sargon inscription says 5,400 men ate daily before him, read as a standing royal army (Westenholz 1999 pp. 65-68, cited in the fetched page); Naram-Sin's inscription names the 'Nine Regiments of Akkad' as the core. Rimush claims 16,212 enemy slain in one battle (royal inscription, quoted in Hamblin 2006, not used as a size). Split: archers ~29%; the Akkadian reliefs introduce the bow (probably composite) into Mesopotamian battle scenes (Lafont et al. 2001 cited in the fetched page).

quality.note: Composite bow, an advanced weapon for 2250 BCE (rubric 0.75).

count.note: Field force of Naram-Sin c. 2250: no modern total exists. Anchors: a Sargon inscription says 5,400 men ate daily before him, read as a standing royal army (Westenholz 1999 pp. 65-68, cited in the fetched page); Naram-Sin's inscription names the 'Nine Regiments of Akkad' as the core. Rimush claims 16,212 enemy slain in one battle (royal inscription, quoted in Hamblin 2006, not used as a size). Split: javelin and skirmish troops, Amorite and highland auxiliaries ~14%.

commandQuality.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: Sargon and Naram-Sin were proven conquerors with generals (shakkanakkum) commanding organized corps; no evidence of a staff system.

cohesion.note: Rubric 0.25-0.5: repeated 'Great Revolt' of Sumerian and Akkadian cities against Naram-Sin; loyal royal core.

morale.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: long run of victories and a divine-king ideology.

weapons.note: Anchor 1 (2500 BCE copper/bronze maces, spears) plus the composite bow seen on Akkadian monuments, a step toward anchor 2.

armor.note: Anchor 1: leather capes and copper helmets; little body armour.

ships.note: Anchor 1: oared riverboats; Sargon claims ships from Meluhha, Magan and Dilmun moored at Akkad (sea trade, not a war fleet).

fortification.note: Anchor 1: mudbrick city walls (Uruk, Ur) and fortified outposts such as Nagar.

logistics.note: Anchor 1: donkeys, onager wagons, river and canal transport; redistributive granaries.

communications.note: Anchor 1: runners and river messengers; Akkadian adopted as an administrative language across the empire.

isr.note: Year anchor (2250 BCE ~ 1.1): scouts and informants.

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison Project 2023 via https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-maddison-project-database.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true: Iraq 1 CE = 1,116 (2011 int$), Iraq 730 CE = 1,466. Applied 2,250 years earlier and scaled down (lower agricultural productivity, no coinage, but highly productive irrigated cereal farming).

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess. The standing army was fed from palace rations; no fiscal data.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess. Craft production (metal, textiles) concentrated in temple and palace workshops.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess. Irrigated barley agriculture in the alluvium produced high yields per seed and fed large dependent workforces.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in a pre-modern age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model as the classical snapshots; Bronze Age life expectancy was if anything lower, so this is not an underestimate.

roadKm.note: Educated guess. No engineered road network is attested; movement followed rivers, canals and caravan tracks.

majorPorts.note: Educated guess. River and Gulf harbours: Akkad quay, Ur, Lagash, Mari on the Euphrates.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess. Gulf trade ships of a few tons to ~20 t and river craft.

supplyRangeKm.note: Educated guess. Armies moved along rivers with boat supply; away from water, donkey trains limited range.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess. ~0.06-0.12 donkeys, oxen and onager hybrids per inhabitant.

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.1: local supply and familiar alluvial terrain; walled cities argue for 1.2, but the cities themselves were the rebels.

notes: Snapshot = reign of Naram-Sin c. 2250 BCE (middle chronology), empire at greatest extent. Archetype doctrine is bronze-chariot but the Akkadian army had no horse chariots: the four-wheeled onager battle-wagons of the Early Dynastic period appear to have lost importance in favour of infantry, so no chariots role is listed. All army numbers are reconstructions; royal inscriptions (5,400 men fed daily; enemy dead in the thousands) are not used as mids. Population convention: everything inside the border, McEvedy-Jones-type regional series interpolated.
